newsitem.title: USA: Alexander looks like running for president again.
newsitem.headline: Alexander looks like running for president again.

text.p: Former Tennessee Gov. Lamar Alexander, who ran for president last year wearing a red and black plaid shirt, sounds like a man planning to do it again.

"I'm delighted to be where I am in the Republican Party. I want to spend the next couple of years helping our party develop its sense of mission and its message more clearly and then I may volunteer to be its messenger once more," Alexander told Reuters in an interview this week.

In his 1996 bid, he came close to breaking through in the New Hampshire primary, where he placed third, only three percentage points behind Bob Dole, the eventual Republican nominee. Conservative columnist Pat Buchanan won the New Hampshire vote.

Dole later said he would have dropped out of the race had he finished third, leaving Alexander to face Buchanan for the nomination. And, according to President Clinton's former political consultant Dick Morris, Alexander was the one Republican the president did not want to face in the election -- the only one he saw as a real threat.

After New Hampshire, Alexander quickly ran out of money and was forced to retire three weeks later. But he said he had learned many lessons from the experience and had built an organisation that would endure.

"Presidential fund raising is two years away. Last time I had no names, this time I have 22,000 names (of potential donors) on my computer," he said. "Last time I had no names in Iowa. This time I have 10,000, many of whom are supporters. Last time I had no names in New Hampshire. This time I have 7,000."
Alexander said no Republican had won his party's presidential nomination on his first attempt since Dwight Eisenhower in 1952.

"This is the first time since World War II that our party doesn't have a dominant political figure. It's wide open. Our grizzled veterans have stepped aside and the troops are sitting around the camp fire ... looking for a mission and looking for a leader," he said.
The key to victory in 2000, as in 1996, will lie in fund raising. "A candidate who runs will have to be able to raise at least $15 million during 1999," Alexander said.

"That's the hard part, to raise it when nobody is paying attention in amounts of $1,000 or less. There will probably only be three or four Republicans who actually are capable of doing that. It's harder than it looks."

One problem for Alexander in 2000 may be the emergence of Tennessee Republican Sen. Fred Thompson as a possible presidential rival from the same state. Thompson will be in the spotlight this year as chairman of upcoming Senate hearings into White House and Democratic fund-raising scandals.

Alexander depended heavily on fund raising from his home state and would again if he ran. The state is probably not big enough to sustain two major candidates, leaving aside the fact that Vice President Al Gore, also from Tennessee, is frontrunner for the Democratic nomination.

For that reason, Alexander is trying to move early to lock in important supporters before Thompson can get organised. But he has his own problem. Early polls of Republican voters show him well down the field in low single digits. As in 1996, he may be the second choice of many but the first choice of few.

Meanwhile, he is working in his private company, which manages child care centres around the country, volunteering for the Salvation Army half a day a week and making occasional trips to key states to chat up potential supporters.
As for the plaid shirt, Alexander denied reports that he would not wear it on the campaign trail if he ran again.
"The plaid shirt is in my closet and I've worn it for years ... I'm not about to lose it," he said.
